Description: The Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster was established with the aim of developing the cybersecurity ecosystem and acting as a bridge between public institutions, the private sector, and academia.
Objective(s): To increase the number of cybersecurity companies in Türkiye.|To support the development of the technical, administrative and financial capabilities of member companies.|To promote the branding of products and services.|To improve the standards of the cybersecurity ecosystem.|To enhance the competitiveness of member companies in the national and global market.|To increase human capital in the field of cybersecurity & Raise awareness about cybersecurity throughout the society.
Background:
The Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster was established with the aim of developing the cybersecurity ecosystem and serving as a bridge between public institutions, the private sector, and academia.
The planning and coordination of the Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster’s activities are carried out by the Cluster Executive Board, which consists of representatives from the Defense Industry Agency (SSB) and the Digital Transformation Office (DTO). The Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster platform primarily aims to create a Türkiye that produces technology in the field of cybersecurity and competes globally. This aligns with its mission to build a national cybersecurity ecosystem, develop local/national cybersecurity products, and promote their widespread use.
The Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster was formed in 2017 with the participation of all public agencies/organizations, representatives from the private sector and academia, and with the support of the Presidency of Defense Industries. On February 1, 2021, a protocol was signed between the Presidency of Defense Industry (SSB) and the Presidency of Digital Transformation Office (DTO) to jointly execute the activities of the Türkiye Cybersecurity Cluster Platform. The Cluster’s planning and coordination are managed by the Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster Executive Board, while the daily operations of the platform are carried out by the Coordination Office.
The Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster Platform operates under five main pillars: Access to Market, Innovation, Access to Talent, Interaction, and Technological Leadership.
Access to Market: To promote the use and competitiveness of local products in both national and global markets, business development activities, including promotional efforts, are conducted. In addition to promoting their activities domestically and internationally, national companies are encouraged to participate in national and international fairs.
Innovation: To discover new ideas in cybersecurity and promote local products with global competitive power, various entrepreneurship competitions, idea challenges, demo days, and hackathons are organized.
Access to Talent : To nurture the human capital required by Türkiye’s cybersecurity ecosystem and improve the qualifications of the existing workforce, training programs are delivered, camps are organized, and competitions are held periodically. Since 2018, over 3,500 students have been trained through these programs, which continued online during the pandemic. Additionally, to discover new talent, HackIstanbul-Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions and graduation project competitions are organized, and young individuals representing Türkiye abroad are supported.
Interaction: To cultivate the cybersecurity ecosystem and bring together all relevant stakeholders under one roof, national and international conferences, sectoral summits, and SIBERKAFE activities are organized. These events foster interaction both within the sector and with other industries.
Technological Leadership: Various working groups have been established to enable cluster members to collaborate, closely follow technological advancements, and conduct studies in areas required by the sector. The Technology Monitoring Working Group has prepared the Turkish Cybersecurity Cluster product, service, and training catalog. The Export Working Group has conducted studies related to international activities. The Test and Certification Working Group is actively developing test and certification criteria for cybersecurity products, aiming to ensure the reliability of local products through testing and certification.

English name: National Research, Development and Innovation Strategy
Original name(s): MAGYARORSZÁG KUTATÁSI, FEJLESZTÉSI ÉS INNOVÁCIÓS STRATÉGIÁJA (2021-2030)
Description: The vision of the Strategy is to achieve a knowledge-based, balanced and sustainable economy and society, generating high added value for all regions within the country.
Objective(s):
Horizontal objectives:
1. Encourage receptivity to innovation, open-mindedness, creative thinking and value creation
2. Establish a modern regulatory framework and business environment supporting RDI activities
3. Strengthen territorial, social and economic cohesion through the system of RDI tools
4. Create a financing system that keeps in mind both stability and incentives
5. Encourage challenge- (mission-) and demand-driven RDI
6. Ensure gender equality within the domestic RDI system.|Overarching goals:
1. Knowledge creation
2. Knowledge flows
3. Knowledge utilisation.
Background:
The Strategy has been accepted by the Government (by Govt. decree No. 1456/2021), and published in the Hungarian Gazette, the official journal of Hungary on July 13, 2021.

The mission of the Strategy is the following
● Contribute to achieving the objectives set out in the vision and address major social challenges by creating a stable and supportive environment.
● Encourage, in the field of academic policy, the creation, maintenance and development of a critical mass of RDI capacities and increased cooperation with the business sector in order to ensure more efficient academic management.
● Support innovation targeted at all organisations, not limited to technological innovation (encompassing research, education and awareness-raising based on scientific and business excellence).
● Promote international integration, in particular within Europe.
● Promote innovation in the public sector.


The Strategy complies with the Government’s RDI policy objective to enhance Hungary’s competitiveness by using RDI resources in a more efficient, conscientious way, in line with strategic objectives.

The ‘Investment in the Future’ National RDI Strategy for the 2013-2020 period is deemed the predecessor (built on the same 3 overarching goals highlighted above) of the present Strategy, providing a good starting point for determining the strategic policy objectives after 2021.
The Smart Specialisation Strategy (S3) is the bridge between the Strategy and the sectoral strategies.

Act LXXVI of 2014 on scientific research, development and innovation stipulates that the Government shall primarily entrust tasks related to the public funding of research, development and innovation to the National Research, Development and Innovation Office.

Original name(s): MAGYARORSZÁG KUTATÁSI, FEJLESZTÉSI ÉS INNOVÁCIÓS STRATÉGIÁJA (2021-2030)
Description: The vision of the Strategy is to achieve a knowledge-based, balanced and sustainable economy and society, generating high added value for all regions within the country.
Objective(s):
Horizontal objectives:
1. Encourage receptivity to innovation, open-mindedness, creative thinking and value creation
2. Establish a modern regulatory framework and business environment supporting RDI activities
3. Strengthen territorial, social and economic cohesion through the system of RDI tools
4. Create a financing system that keeps in mind both stability and incentives
5. Encourage challenge- (mission-) and demand-driven RDI
6. Ensure gender equality within the domestic RDI system.|Overarching goals:
1. Knowledge creation
2. Knowledge flows
3. Knowledge utilisation.
Background:
The Strategy has been accepted by the Government (by Govt. decree No. 1456/2021), and published in the Hungarian Gazette, the official journal of Hungary on July 13, 2021.

The mission of the Strategy is the following
● Contribute to achieving the objectives set out in the vision and address major social challenges by creating a stable and supportive environment.
● Encourage, in the field of academic policy, the creation, maintenance and development of a critical mass of RDI capacities and increased cooperation with the business sector in order to ensure more efficient academic management.
● Support innovation targeted at all organisations, not limited to technological innovation (encompassing research, education and awareness-raising based on scientific and business excellence).
● Promote international integration, in particular within Europe.
● Promote innovation in the public sector.


The Strategy complies with the Government’s RDI policy objective to enhance Hungary’s competitiveness by using RDI resources in a more efficient, conscientious way, in line with strategic objectives.

The ‘Investment in the Future’ National RDI Strategy for the 2013-2020 period is deemed the predecessor (built on the same 3 overarching goals highlighted above) of the present Strategy, providing a good starting point for determining the strategic policy objectives after 2021.
The Smart Specialisation Strategy (S3) is the bridge between the Strategy and the sectoral strategies.

Description: S3 is a specific, territorially-based and sector-oriented policy instrument, a dynamic, medium-term umbrella strategy contributing to the achievement of the EU Cohesion Policy Objective 1 (Smarter Europe through innovation and support for economic transformation and modernisation) for the 2021-2027 programming (budgetary) period.
Objective(s):
S3 sets out, based on the entrepreneurial discovery process (EDP), the following national economic priorities for the national economy on which Hungary will focus in pursuing smart specialisation:
• Cutting-edge technologies
• Health
• Digitisation of the economy
• Energy, climate
• Services
• Resource-efficient economy
• Agriculture, food industry
• Creative industry.|In addition to the above 8 national economic priorities, 2 horizontal priorities have been selected:
• Training, education
• Public sector and university innovation.
Background:
S3 is a planning document helping develop a complex concept for economic development. In order for Hungary to become one of Europe’s strong innovators, in addition to increasing resources and R&D expenditure on business development, it is also necessary to plan and use EU and domestic funding in a results-oriented and more efficient way.


The Strategy has been accepted by the Government (by Govt. decree No. 1428/2021)), and published in the Hungarian Gazette, the official journal of Hungary on July 2, 2021.


S3 can be seen as an umbrella strategy for the following three national policy planning documents:
• National RDI Strategy 2021-2030
• SME Strategy (2019-2030)
• National Digitisation Strategy (2021-2030).

One of the key elements of the S3 methodology is the use of entrepreneurial discovery process (EDP) in the design of specialisation directions.

English name: TÜBİTAK 1607 - BiGG+ SME Mentorship Interface Program
Original name(s): TÜBİTAK 1607 - BiGG+ KOBİ Mentor Arayüzü Programı
Description: The BiGG+ SME Mentorship Interface Program aims to enhance the business development and innovation capacities of SMEs by establishing and implementing structured mentorship mechanisms. The program facilitates commercialization, market expansion, and export growth for SMEs previously supported by TÜBİTAK by providing expert mentorship in business strategy, technology adoption, and innovation management.
Objective(s): To enhance the competitive power of SMEs in domestic and international markets by promoting their innovative products, developed with TÜBİTAK R&D and innovation support, through a qualified mentoring mechanism.
Background:
The BiGG+ SME Mentorship Interface Call was launched in 2022 with the goal of establishing structured mentorship mechanisms to strengthen the innovation and commercialization capacities of SMEs. The program was introduced as part of TÜBİTAK's efforts to optimize the allocation of public resources in research and innovation by facilitating SME access to expert mentorship and business advisory services.
Over the past two years, the program has expanded significantly, engaging various regional and national organizations such as Technology Development Zones (TDZs), Technology Transfer Offices (TTOs), and private mentorship firms.
SMEs receiving mentoring services are expected to achieve improvements in the following areas:
• Increase in turnover
• Increase in current market share
• Entry into new markets
• Overseas sales or an increase in current overseas sales
As of 2024, a total of 18 mentorship interfaces have been supported, with a combined budget allocation of 60,314,708 TL. The number of SMEs benefiting from the program has increased from 1,462 in 2022 to 1,805 in 2024, with measurable impacts on their revenue growth, market expansion, and international competitiveness.
The focus of the program has also evolved, placing greater emphasis on sector-specific mentorship models and regional innovation clusters. In the 2022 Call, mentorship support was expanded to include a sustainability theme and EIC Accelerator preparations.

Objective(s): To value scientific and technological knowledge, optimising its transfer to companies and its transformation into innovation.|To improve coordination between the different actors in the Innovation system: Higher Education Institutions, TICs and companies.|To ensure core funding for TICs that play a relevant role in technology transfer and empower companies in their transition to a circular economy, namely by contributing to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and, thus, to the mitigation of climate change.|To increase R&D (Research and Development) and Innovation capacity in small and medium-sized companies, enhancing their connection to the innovation system through TICs.|To promote innovation leading to an efficient and productive use of material and energy resources through TIC.;|To facilitate the access of TICs and companies to highly qualified human resources, promoting qualified employment.
Background:
This initiative was set in 2016 with the assumption that stimulating creativity and innovation in all domains is essential to successfully respond to social, economic and environmental challenges.

Since 2024, a shift in the focus of the fund has been decided, with resources being allocated to entrepreneurial activities - support to start-ups and scale-ups aligned with the mission of the fund, through seed funding, vouchers and a deep tech fund, to be launched in 2025.

Original name(s): Estratégia Regional de Especialização Inteligente do Centro
Description: Centro’s Smart Specialisation Strategy defines the regional priorities for research and innovation. It is a strategic framework to align regional agents own strategies and guide concentration of resources on the identified priorities.

Within each of these areas, lines of action were defined as transformative agendas to be persued.
Background:
In the previous programming period (2014-2020) the definition of a Smart Specialisation Strategy was an ex-ante conditionality of the Cohesion Policy. Considering the beginning of a new programming period and the new challenges faced, Centro RIS3 was revised, mostly during the year of 2020. The updated documents were approved by the Coordinating Council in April 2021.

Description: Increasing capacities in innovation management for companies.
Objective(s): Support companies that prioritize innovation as a growth strategy through the development of capacities in innovation management, increased investment in ACTI and generation and strengthening of connections between actors of the STI system.|Integrate the knowledge generated through STI activities in the country, in order to generate innovation processes in the business sector.|Training in innovation for the generation of innovation capacities in companies and construction or strengthening of business innovation systems.|Financing of innovation projects for companies in the territories according to the specific needs of each region.|Training, advisory, consulting or technological services activities that are focused on promoting levels of technological maturity, in accordance with the needs to generate R & D & I capacities in the beneficiaries.
Background:
This Instrument began through a Pilot between 2011 and 2012, through calls 534-2011 and 577-2012 aimed at entrepreneurs. The Innovation Management Capacity Building Program was part of the credit operation with the Inter-American Development Bank -IDB and the World Bank - WB.
In 2013 and 2014, Colciencias designed the instrument "locomotive of innovation for companies" through which it selected organizations to receive government support in innovation projects. By integrating knowledge and methodologies from national and international expert teams and financing resources, companies developed innovative products, services or business models that incorporated knowledge and technology.

In 2015, an impact assessment was carried out through an external company to determine the effectiveness of Colciencias innovation locomotive, through the definition of a baseline, the design and initial implementation of the impact assessment in relation to the economic performance and productivity of the companies financed , as well as the aggregation of business capabilities in innovation and the implementation of product, service or business model innovation processes based on scientific or technological knowledge. From this evaluation, benefits and good practices for adjusting the instrument were identified.

Between 2015 -2018 the Strategy of Pacts for Innovation is deployed, which is led by Colciencias and operated through alliances and joint efforts with the Chambers of Commerce. A pact was signed with eight regions of the country.

In 2019, the Pacts for Innovation strategy is renewed, and a new portfolio of benefits adapted for each region is created: acceleration program, open innovation, innovation community, young researchers and innovators in innovation systems, conference cycles, among others. Special cooperation agreements are signed to join forces with the Chambers of Commerce.

Description: The Recognition of Actors initiative aims to formally identify and validate the capacities of groups, institutions, and innovation units that participate in science, technology, and innovation activities within Colombia’s National System of Science, Technology, and Innovation (SNCTI). This process ensures that recognized actors—such as research centers and institutes, technological development centers, Technology Transfer Offices (TTOs), highly innovative enterprises, business R&D&i units, technology-based business incubators, innovation and productivity centers; science, technology, or innovation Parks; and science centers—are eligible to compete for public funding and strategic opportunities. Recognition strengthens the visibility, credibility, and articulation of these actors within the national and international STI ecosystem.
Objective(s): To promote a favorable environment for the organization of the National System of Science, Technology, and Innovation (SNCTI) through the establishment of guidelines and incentives that foster specialization and the pursuit of excellence among its actors. To this end, the Ministry sets out strategies and guidelines to be implemented in the short and medium term through the evaluation of the strategic, interrelation, resource, and results dimensions of each actor seeking recognition.
Background: The recognition of actors in the National Science, Technology, and Innovation System (SNCTeI) has historically been a key mechanism to strengthen the system’s structure and to ensure that individuals and organizations engaged in STI activities can access public funding and strategic opportunities. Since the early 1990s, successive calls and regulatory frameworks have defined standards for identifying research groups, research centers, technological development centers, and other actors contributing to knowledge production and innovation in Colombia. Over the years, recognition processes evolved to incorporate stricter quality standards, broader categories of actors, and mechanisms to foster transparency and inclusivity. The official recognition of actors policy dates from 2016. Today, the recognition not only certifies technical capacities but also serves as a tool to map the country’s innovation ecosystem and to support the design of evidence-based public policies. In 2024, activities began to include new actors in the recognition process, specifically science- and technology-based enterprises and community-based organizations. As part of the modernization process, efforts are currently underway to update the recognition framework.

Description: The Marie Sklodowska Curie Actions (MSCA) is a research and training programme that supports the career, skills development, and mobility of researchers at all stages of their careers and from all over the world.
Objective(s): MSCA contribute to excellent research, boosting jobs, growth and investment by equipping researchers with new knowledge and skills, and foster research cooperation across borders, sectors and disciplines.|Intersectoral mobility and collaboration has always been at the heart of the MSCA programme. Exposure to different sectors, notably through secondments and other hosting arrangements, as well transferable skills building are imbedded in the research and training activities of all MSCA actions.
Background:
The MSCA contribute, inter alia to the development of excellent doctoral programmes, postdoctoral training programmes and collaborative research projects.
This is done through the following key MSCA actions:
- The MSCA Doctoral Networks aim to train creative, entrepreneurial, innovative and resilient doctoral candidates, able to face current and future challenges and to convert knowledge and ideas into products and services for economic and social benefit. Doctoral Networks implement doctoral programmes by partnerships of organisations from different sectors across Europe and beyond to train highly skilled doctoral candidates, stimulate their creativity, enhance their innovation capacities and boost their employability in the long-term. Besides standard Doctoral Networks, incentives have been introduced to promote two specific types of doctorates as well. Industrial Doctorates. They train PhD candidates who wish develop their skills and step outside academia, in particular in industry and business. Individual participants must be enrolled in a doctoral programme and jointly supervised by the academic and non-academic partners. Joint Doctorates. They provide a highly integrated type of international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration in doctoral training leading to a joint doctoral degree or multiple doctoral degrees awarded by the participating institutions. PhD candidates must be enrolled in a joint programme and be jointly supervised.
- The MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships aim to enhance the creative and innovative potential of researchers holding a PhD, wishing to acquire new skills through advanced training, international, interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral mobility. Through the implementation of an original and personalised research project, MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships aim to foster excellence through training and mobility. There are 2 types of Postdoctoral Fellowships: a) European Postdoctoral Fellowships. They are open to researchers moving within Europe or coming to Europe from another part of the world to pursue their research career. These fellowships take place in an EU Member State or Horizon Europe Associated Country and can last between 1 and 2 years. Researchers of any nationality can apply, b) Global Postdoctoral Fellowships. They fund the mobility of researchers outside Europe. The fellowship lasts between 2 to 3 years, of which the first 1 to 2 years will be spent in a non-associated Third Country, followed by a mandatory return phase of 1 year to an organisation based in an EU Member State or Horizon Europe Associated Country. Only nationals or long-term residents of the EU Member States or Horizon Europe Associated Countries can apply. Under Horizon Europe, Postdoctoral Fellowships are implementing an incentive in an effort to build bridges between the academic and non-academic sector (that includes private sector): researchers can receive additional support to carry out a placement of up to 6 months in a non-academic organisation based in an EU Member State or Horizon Europe Associated Country. This placement needs to take place at the end of their fellowship.
- MSCA COFUND co-finances new or existing doctoral programmes and postdoctoral fellowship schemes at national, regional or international level with the aim to spread the best practices of the MSCA including international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary research training, as well as international and cross-sectoral mobility of researchers at all stages of their career.

Description: Moonshot aims to realise technological breakthroughs by 2040, both in products and processes, which in turn can contribute to achieving the climate objectives in an economically viable context by 2050. The Flemish Climate Jump is developed as a coordinating action program for industrial climate transition, addressing both process transformations and infrastructure and energy needs.
Objective(s): Industrial Decarbonization: Supporting companies in reducing CO2 emissions through process transformations and energy-efficient technologies. // Cluster-Based Approach: Encouraging collaboration between energy-intensive industries to optimize resource sharing, such as residual heat recovery.|Infrastructure Development: Creating essential infrastructure like hydrogen networks, heat grids, CO2 capture and transport systems, and renewable energy integration. // Competitiveness & Sustainability: Ensuring international competitive positioning while committing to long-term sustainability goals.|Policy Coordination & Monitoring: Establishing clear roadmaps and sector-specific goals, with annual progress evaluations and adjustments. // Long-Term Vision (2050): Developing a structured transition framework with concrete milestones for achieving climate neutrality.
Background:
With the Moonshot project, Flanders wants to play a pioneering role in innovation by pursuing fundamental breakthroughs in the next two decades in basic research at the knowledge institutes and then applying them in the energy-intensive industries (primarily chemistry, refining and steel).
This demand-driven long-term vision makes government, research and business allies for a successful climate approach. In 2020, for the second time an application round was organised for projects in Moonshot "Flanders CO2 neutral".

Klimaatsprong is a coordinating action program initiated by the Flemish Government to accelerate industrial climate transition. It builds on previous research efforts, such as Moonshot Vlaanderen, but shifts towards practical implementation by integrating technology, infrastructure, and policy coordination.

The Flemish Government approved the first program document (Programme Klimaatsprong) in June 2023. It runs until 2025 and includes short- and long-term actions up to 2050. Every five years, a new program document is presented, evaluating the previous one and outlining the approach for the next five years. The next program document is scheduled for 2025.

Background:
I-Corps@SFI is a unique partnership between SFI and the NSF Innovation Corps (NSF I-Corps). I-Corps@SFI has the overarching ambition to increase the number of researchers in Ireland using the NSF I-Corps evidence-based entrepreneurship methodology to validate the impact potential of research ideas and, thereby, increase the quality of teams translating research for economic and societal impact. I-Corps@SFI comprises two elements: the I-Corps@SFI Academy and the SFI/NSF I-Corps@SFI Entrepreneurial Training Programme (ETP). The I-Corps@SFI Academy sets out to provide training for researchers in evidence-based entrepreneurship that prepares them to apply to the SFI/NSF I-Corps@SFI Entrepreneurial Training Programme (ETP). It also provides training to technology transfer office (TTO) and other University/Institute of Technology staff to deliver evidence-based entrepreneurship training to researchers locally to better prepare researchers for later downstream supports.

Under I-Corps@SFI, SFI launched two calls of the ETP in 2016 and 2018, which provided training support for 13 academic research teams (comprising 39 individuals). In 2021, the I-Corps@SFI Academy was launched and has provided training support for 20 teams (comprising 60 individuals) or which 20 were TTO/ University/Institute of Technology staff.

In 2024, following the merger of SFI and the IRC into Research-Ireland, Research Ireland took over the administration of the programme.

English name: The Strategic Intervention Lines on Industrial Property for the Three-Year Period 2021-2023
Original name(s): Le Linee di intervento strategiche sulla proprietà industriale per il triennio 2021-2023
Description: The Ministry of Economic Development of Italy has published in July 2021 the Strategic Intervention Lines on Property 2021-2023, the first start in the implementation of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan: the document traces a challenging and decidedly ambitious path to strengthen the protection and respect of industrial property in Italy.
Objective(s): The strategy will define actions necessary to respond to five challenges to strengthen the protection and respect of industrial property rights: improve the IP protection system; encourage the use and dissemination of IP, in particular by SMEs; easy access and sharing of intangible assets, while ensuring a fair return on investment; guarantee the strictest respect for industrial property; strengthen Italy's role in European and international fora on industrial property. The plan has a very wide scope, and is divided into a long series of macro-objectives concerning every aspect of industrial property, including an IP regime reform (patent and trademark law)
Background:
the strategy defines the updating of the legislation on industrial property, with the preparation of a bill revising the Industrial Property Code (CPI). The revision of the implementing regulation of the CPI, envisaged by the Strategic Lines, has just been launched with the decree of 1 June 2021 n. 119, effective from 9 September 2021.

Among the objectives of the revision is the adoption of the new European regulation of industrial design rights, in the sign of the transition to the digital economy and the consequent affirmation of new types of design such as graphic interfaces, holograms and virtual / augmented reality.

In the field of patents, it is intended, among other things, to allow the applicant to obtain the right to protection of the invention from the moment the application is filed (based on the so-called first to deposit principle), allowing the payment of taxes of filing within a term following the submission of the application, thus aligning the Italian legislation with that of other European countries.

As regards the distinctive signs, the aim will also be to promote greater harmonization between the protection of trademarks and agricultural geographical indications - among other things probing the possibility of excluding from registration the trademarks evocative of geographical indications and designations of origin recognized by the law - and elaborate proposals for the introduction of the protection of geographical indications for non-agricultural products

Description: The Slovenian Scientific Research and Innovation Strategy 2030 is a key strategic document for research, development, and innovation. Background: ReZrIS30 is based on the outputs and guidelines adopted by the Science and Technology Council of the Republic of Slovenia (STC) on 20 January 2021. It addresses key societal, international, and national challenges, as well as organisational challenges. The objectives consider the emerging framework of the European Research Area (ERA), where national policies in research and innovation (R&I) are developed with regard to broader geographical aspects and the internationalisation of research. English name: Body of Experts on Industrial Property
Description: On request, the body, operating under the supervision of the Hungarian Intellectual Property Office (SzTNH), gives expert opinions covering the widest possible range of issues arising from the exercise of rights in the protection of industrial property (IP).

Background:
The measure of the scientific technological development, the requirements of the approximation of laws at the international and especially at the European Community level are a great challenge to the regulation of intellectual property (IP) rights. It has become necessary for the judicial system (e.g. courts and authorities) to request opinions issued by expert bodies whose members have up-to-date knowledge on IP when ruling on a specific case.

The body was established by Govt. Decree No 270/2002 (XII. 20.) on the Structure and Operation of the Body of Experts on IP.

English name: Reforming the Science, Research and Innovation System - Setting Up a New Regulatory Framework
Original name(s): Reformiranje znanstvenoraziskovalnega in inovacijskega sistema - vzpostavitev novih zakonskih podlag
Description: The main solutions of the law aim to ensure the conditions for the development of high-quality and globally comparable scientific research activities. This is achieved by providing a basis for adequate and stable funding of public research organisations, opportunities for rewarding excellent researchers, open access to scientific publications and research data, and ensuring a high level of ethics and integrity in science. Additionally, the law stipulates that public research organisations may establish companies for the purpose of transferring knowledge to society or the economy, and it establishes conditions for more effective strategic planning and guidance of scientific research activities at the national level. Amendments to the Act are foreseen in 2025, focusing on improving the evaluation of recipients of stable funding, considering the quality of institutional frameworks and knowledge transfer.
Objective(s): Ensure a modern scientific research and innovation system that enhances quality of life by addressing societal issues and increasing economic competitiveness.|Promote effective governance of the research and innovation system, and encourage the popularisation of science, creativity, and innovation in society and education.|Foster excellent research in the public sector.|Build capacity to support research and innovation through human resources, specialisation, and infrastructure for an innovative economy.|Ensure stable and adequate public funding for research and development.
Background: To actively co-create the new European Research Area and compete with the best, Slovenia needs to reform its scientific research and innovation system. A new law, the Scientific Research and Innovation Activity Act, was adopted and came into force on 1 January 2022. Additionally, the Slovenian Scientific Research and Innovation Strategy 2030, the Research Infrastructure Roadmap 2030, the Strategy for the Internationalisation of Higher Education and Science in the Republic of Slovenia 2030, and the Action Plan for Open Science have been adopted, along with relevant sub-legislative acts. Scientific research activities will be based on the principles of open science, ensuring that research results are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, while also employing responsible metrics for assessment and involving communities and citizen science. An Action Plan to implement Objective 5, focusing on accelerating science-business cooperation, knowledge transfer, and innovation, is set for 2025.

Description: The University may establish single-person capital companies – "special purpose vehicles" for the purpose of indirect commercialization, consisting in taking up or acquiring shares in companies or taking up subscription warrants entitling to subscribe for or take up shares in companies, in order to implement or prepare for implementation the results of scientific activity or know-how related to these results, in accordance with Article 148 of the Act of 20 July 2018. Law on Higher Education
Objective(s): Support pre-implementation work, including additional laboratory tests or adapting the invention to the needs of the interested buyer.|Support the preparation of projects for the commercialization of the results of scientific research and development works, including analyses of the market potential of inventions and analysis of their readiness for implementation, as well as valuation of industrial property rights.|Support the cooperation between the scientific community and the economic environment, including searching for entities interested in the implementation of research results, through the promotion of the technological offer and participation in exhibitions and fairs.|Support technology portfolio management, including, inter alia, monitoring and analysis of research results in terms of their usefulness, analysis of market needs and examination of the state of the art before starting research, analysis of the possibilities of obtaining patent protection and the possibility of commercialization of research and development results.|Support the identification of innovation brokers, acting as intermediaries operating in specific areas of knowledge, responsible for establishing cooperation between the scientific community and the economic environment.
Background:
Spin -off is created as a result of research activities of academics employed at universities. With the help of such a company, the university has a chance to commercialize research results, and thus — attract new investors. The founder of this type of unit is a researcher, student or university graduate. Such a company uses the intellectual goods of the university.
It is also a way to create new, highly specialized jobs for graduates. The appearance of companies in the vicinity of the university using the results of its employees' research allows access to additional funds for research and implementation, and also creates favorable conditions for increasing revenues from the commercialization of the results of these studies.
The problems of a spin-off associated with a scientific institution may be: a source of financing, technology transfer from university to company, as well as access to modern technologies. Issues such as intellectual property law (patents, licenses) or relations with the university are also mentioned.
According to data collected by the Information Processing Centre of the National Research Institute (OPI), in September 2022 there are currently 102 special purpose vehicles operating at universities.
The Ministry of Education and Science supports the process of commercialization of the results of scientific research and development work. The aim of the Innovation Incubator program is to increase the impact of scientific achievements on the development of innovation and to intensify cooperation between the scientific community and the economic environment. The support is addressed to HEIs and special purpose vehicles established by HEIs. It is also possible to create consortia whose leaders are the above-mentioned entities. A member of the consortium may be a university, a special purpose vehicle established within it, a company established by the institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences and a company established by a research institute.
Responsible organisation(s): Agency for Enterprise Development (PARP;Polska Agencja Rozwoju Przedsiębiorczości)

English name: Code of Practice on the Management of Intellectual Assets for Knowledge Valorisation
Description: The code of practice on the management of intellectual assets for knowledge valorisation aims to increase the use of research results and accelerate the uptake of innovative technologies by leveraging intellectual assets, including intellectual property.
Objective(s): Provide comprehensive recommendations and addresses specific challenges faced by research and innovation stakeholders such as the efficient management of intellectual assets in joint research activities and the development of research and innovation activities in open science and open innovation contexts.
Background:
In line with the guiding principles, the Code of practice goes beyond formal intellectual property (IP) rights and offers guidance for the management of other types of intellectual assets.

Intellectual assets are not limited to IP rights, but include any result or products generated by research and innovation activities such as publications, data and know-how to maximise value creation opportunities.

The Code of practice was co-created with experienced stakeholders through a dedicated community of practice over a six-month period and was subject to a consultation of ERA Forum members during a workshop in September 2022.

English name: Code of Practice on Standardisation in the European Research Area
Description: The new code of practice on standardisation aims to contribute to the successful integration of research and innovation with standardisation.
Objective(s): Provide guidance to researchers and innovators by, for example, identifying elements of good practice.
Background:
The new code of practice on standardisation concerns research and innovation activities without any technology boundaries. It targets research and innovation actors within a wide range of technology readiness levels from terminologies and concepts, through testing to interoperability and performance.

The Code of practice is a hands-on guidance that provides a set of recommendations grouped under 3 sections:

- For higher education institutions and research and innovation organisations to build relevant capacities;
- For beneficiaries of EU, national and local research and innovation programmes to take inspiration from best practices;
- For the policy level, including European, national and local authorities and standards development organisations, to take into account recommendations that will help everyone to use standardisation as an effective tool to harness results from research and innovation projects.

Description: RDIE focus areas are the areas of research and development, innovation and entrepreneurship that are prioritised in cooperation between the state, enterprises and research institutions in line with Estonia’s development needs and opportunities. The focus areas are central to achieving the objectives of the RDIE Strategy 2021-2035.
Objective(s):
Digital solutions across all areas of life.
With the support of research and development, innovation, and entrepreneurship:
- the digital solutions are created, offered, and used in all areas of life;
- data economy is used to create new business opportunities;
- a secure cyberspace is ensured.|Health technologies and services.
With the support of research and development, innovation, and entrepreneurship:
- more effective and accessible healthcare services are developed and provided;
- efforts are made to offer more patient-centered and evidence-based treatment and prevention, and personalized health services are developed;
- the export potential of healthcare is increased.|Valorisation of local resources - food, wood, mineral, secondary raw materials and waste.

With the support of research and development, innovation, and entrepreneurship local resources are managed sustainably, with consideration for biodiversity and high resource efficiency, focusing on both primary and secondary raw materials, while enhancing the bio- and circular economy.|Smart and sustainable energy solutions.

With the support of research and development, innovation, and entrepreneurship:
- Estonia produces energy in a climate-neutral way;
- Estonia's energy use becomes more efficient and resource-saving;
- efforts are made to ensure energy security.
Background:
The knowledge transfer axis reduces the disconnection of research from the economy and society by leveraging the societal benefits (efficiency) of RDI and triggering the necessary changes, including a significant increase in the added value of the Estonian economy. Bringing about structural change requires synergies between research, business and policymaking, and the pooling of activities and financial resources.

In 2022, roadmaps for the four focus areas were co-created with the representatives of research and development system, entrepreneurship and government entities.

Prioritisation means that the aim is to increase the importance of these sectors in the Estonian economy, including in exports, and in meeting development needs, and that the government provides the additional support for research and development activities required for this.

On the one hand, the focus areas contribute to addressing Estonia’s development needs and, on the other hand, they enable better use of the strengths of Estonian enterprises and research. They have a high commercial potential or a strong global impact. The focus areas are not sectoral, but focused on a development need or opportunity, interdisciplinary and based on cooperation between different fields and sectors (academic, private and public).

RDIE focus areas (including four smart specialisation areas) are integral part of RDIE Strategy and Estonian RDI system and thus subject to RDIE governance. Each focus area will have a road-map, including targets and critical key-actions. Co-design and co-creation (entrepreneurial discovery process) with respective stakeholders and monitoring on a yearly bases is essential part of the RDIE focus areas and activities within these focus areas. Activities within the RDIE focus areas involve RDI missions as tool for increased directionality for the entrepreneurial discovery process.

Description: The 12th Development Plan, approved by the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye at the end of October 2023, sets the main science, technology, and innovation policies for the 2024-2028 period. This plan serves as the primary public policy roadmap, covering all governmental institutions regarding the preparation processes of strategies and action plans. The plan aims to improve the country's position in the international arena and enhance its welfare, including goals for R&D and innovation, as well as other sectors.
Objective(s): To improve the capacity and quality of human resources in the fields of science, technology, and innovation.|To increase the scientific research capacity of universities and strengthen their roles in R&D and innovation activities.|To make research infrastructures more effective with a structure that conducts frontier research by employing qualified human resources and working in collaboration with the private sector.|To develop mechanisms for increasing the transfer of knowledge and technology through collaborations between universities, research infrastructures, and the private sector.|To enhance and expand support for accelerating the development and commercialization of technological products and to support frontier research and technologies that will increase the value-added production.|To transform the R&D and innovation support system into a structure that is focused, performance-based, covering the entire process from research to commercialization, and taking into account the needs and development potential of sectors, especially priority sectors. Also, to develop impact analysis and performance-based methods for resource allocation.
Background:
The 12th Development Plan , adopted by the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye, is the main policy document of the country for the period between 2024 and 2028. The Plan was adopted on October 31, 2023 and sets out the national development policy with a multi-sectoral approach.

The 12th Development Plan of Türkiye (2024-2028) outlines the country’s strategic vision for research, development, and innovation, emphasizing the importance of green and digital transformation to enhance global competitiveness and achieve sustainable development goals. The plan prioritizes the development of a production ecosystem that is environmentally friendly, disaster-resilient, and based on high value-added technologies. The plan highlights critical technologies, including Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data, Quantum Technologies, Cybersecurity, Advanced Materials, Robotics, Micro/Nano/Opto-electronics and Chips, Biotechnology, Hydrogen Technologies, Genome Editing, and Next-Generation Nuclear Reactors. These technologies are identified as enablers for achieving sustainable development goals, addressing global challenges such as climate change and energy transition, and supporting Türkiye’s long-term economic and social development.

Description: The Transfer and Collaboration Plan was born with the aim of strengthening the links between the public and private sectors in research, development and innovation (RDI), to increase the impact of public investment in research and boost the innovative capacity of Spanish companies
Objective(s): Transfer of knowledge generated in the public research system to companies, the public sector and society, through different channels such as the creation of new companies, patent licences, the dissemination of publications or scientific advice.|Encourage the collaboration of companies with universities, other higher education centers and public research centers during the knowledge generation phase, not only through specific collaboration projects for innovation, but also through new, more ambitious models of public-private alliances, as well as through the mobility of research staff and citizen science.|Improve training of research, technical and management personnel in relation to the valorization of knowledge, as well as enhance the connections of the ecosystem, paying special attention to the role of technology centers, knowledge transfer offices, and other intermediate agents and platforms that help the interaction of the actors of the innovation system.
Background:
The Plan proposes new initiatives and reinforces actions initiated in the last two years, many of which are part of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (PRTR), and complements recent regulatory reforms such as the Law of Science, Technology and Innovation (LCTI), the Law for the Promotion of the Ecosystem of Emerging Companies (startups) and the Organic Law of the University System (LOSU).

The implementation will initially be done in two phases. In a first phase, until the end of 2023, the essential measures of the plan will be implemented and the monitoring criteria will be established. During the second phase, until 2025, all the planned initiatives will be executed, additional measures will be initiated, where appropriate, and the results will be evaluated with the aim of introducing the necessary reforms and consolidating the most effective measures, which go beyond 2025. However the spirit of this Plan is to endure over time, incorporating new initiatives in the medium-long term that contribute to achieve the objectives set.

Description: The initiative aims to enhance technological competitivness, sourverinity and acceptance in the realm of digital and key technologies (such as photonics, quantum technology or robotics).
Objective(s):
The objectives of the BMIMI (Federal Ministry of Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure) in this initiative are:
1) Technology sovereignty and open technology solutions
Digital and key technologies should be enhanced in order to develop and
strengthen European value networks. The aim is to drive the development of
cutting-edge technologies and expand existing areas of strength.
2) Achieving technology acceptance and developing ecosystems
The aim is to create acceptance for the application of digital and key
technologies, and to encourage the establishment and further development
of flexible and collaborative creative ecosystems. These should be designed
to support collaboration between different actors and thus promote the
development and use of digital and key technologies.
3) Tackling societal challenges
Promoting digital and key technologies helps tackle societal challenges such
as climate and demographic change, and strengthen democracy and societal
resilience. The Call focuses on digital technologies designed to meet
challenges in the health sector.
Virtual Worlds and Digital Solutions for Health – Topic 1 (English) Page 5/11
4) Competence and capacity building
A strong focus is on developing competencies and capacities, supporting
young talent, and promoting diversity and gender equality in the field of
digital and key technologies. This provides a multi-perspective view on the
project and the resulting products.
Background:
Through application orientation, further technology development should be linked to overcoming societal challenges such as climate change, resource availability or aging and thus also contribute to the transformative RTI priorities of climate-neutral cities, mobility transition, energy transition and circular economy.
This requires the establishment and further development of flexible, cooperative and creative ecosystems by the BMIMI in which a variety of different actors work together. With the increased involvement of different disciplines, sustainable solutions are to be developed and validated.
National funding is intended to strengthen companies and research institutions and initiate transformation processes.

The initiative builds on the long standing experience of bottom-up funding of innovative activities of Austrian companies, in particular SMEs, by the BMWET In the course of implementing the new governance structure based on the FoFinAG the initiative provides a range of funding instruments addressing various needs and innovation barriers.

Original name(s): Plan de Recuperación, Transformación y Resiliencia
Description:
The Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (PRTR) is the national plan developed by Spain to be eligible for the NextGeberationEU Recovery Plan for Europe and to channel the funds allocated by Europe to repair the damage caused by the COVID-19 crisis and to increase productivity and potential growth, moving towards a green, digital, inclusive Spain, with greater social and territorial cohesion and without gender gaps.
The PRTR was approved in July 2021 and is structured around four cross-cutting axes that are specified in 10 policy levers and 31 components that articulate the major investment programme with a 2026 horizon and structural and legislative reforms aimed at addressing the main challenges of our country. Each component focuses on a specific challenge or objective and includes reforms and investments that, in a coherent and complementary way, contribute to achieving these objectives or overcoming the challenges. For all of them, intermediate goals and milestones, expected results, the number of beneficiaries, as well as the detailed cost of each element are identified.
On October 2, 2023, the European Commission issued its favorable report for the second phase of the Recovery Plan and on October 17, 2023, ECOFIN approved it. The Addendum will allow the mobilization of all resources allocated to Spain from the Next Generation EU funds, concentrating additional investments and reforms on strengthening the strategic autonomy of Spain and Europe.
Objective(s): The Recovery Plan responds to a triple objective: (i) to boost activity and job creation to counteract the impact of the pandemic in the short term, (ii) to support a process of structural transformation that will allow for an increase in potential growth in the medium term, and (iii) to strengthen resilience in the long term, moving towards more sustainable and inclusive development.|The aim of the Addendum is to strengthen strategic autonomy by acting on all fronts: i) increasing energy autonomy, based on the transition towards a sustainable and self-sufficient energy model; ii) intensifying agro-food autonomy, to increase the productivity, profitability and sustainability of the sector, with efficient management of natural resources; iii) strengthening industrial autonomy; iv) technological autonomy, bringing production closer to the points of consumption to avoid shortages in critical moments such as the current one and reducing dependence on key materials and technologies; and v) digital security and autonomy, strengthening cybersecurity, improving preparation for more frequent threats and with greater severity in their consequences.
Background: The 4 cross-cutting axes are fully aligned with the EU strategic agendas, the 2030 Agenda and the UN Sustainable Development Goals, as well as with the PNIEC, the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNACC) 2021-2030 and a Spanish Circular Economy Strategy. The addendum is aligned with the challenges identified within the framework of the European Semester, specifically in the specific recommendations (Country Specific Recommendations (CSR) addressed to Spain since 2019, and taking into account in particular the 2023 Country Report .

Description: The BMBF’s "Strategy for Participation in Research" is intended to improve the conditions for public involvement in research and research policy in order to make better use of its added value for innovation policy and society .
Objective(s):
The BMBF‘s Strategy for Participation in Research aims at taking greater advantage of synergies from different participatory research approaches; learning from one another and structure knowledge; further professionalising the field, for example with a view to gauging impact; intensifying capacity building; and firmly anchoring participation in the scientific reputation system as part of good scientific practice.

The following measures are intended to support participation in research and research policy:|A participation network is to be developed to connect mostly decentralised participation communities based on their needs in order to support communication and knowledge transfer. With this aim, the BMBF launched funding in 2022 for the annual PartWiss conference for participation in science. Since spring 2023, the Society for Transdisciplinary and Participatory Research (GTPF) has also been strengthening cooperation between actors in transdisciplinary and participatory research. This contributes to quality assurance, support of young researchers and the visibility of these research approaches.|A guide for research funders and guidelines for researchers may offer practical advice.|The representation of civil society in committees and strategic processes is to be further strengthened.|Support measures for the different research approaches and traditions will be intensified.|In order for participatory projects to be credible and in view of the resources needed for participatory projects, it is vital that the results are used in a transparent and effective manner. It is also recommended that the voluntary commitment of citizens should be properly appreciated so that contributing to research which addresses social challenges remains attractive in the long term for those involved.
Background: With the publication of the "BMBF Policy Paper on Participation" in 2016, the BMBF has committed itself to promoting a high-quality participation of society in research and innovation policy as well as in research itself. The goals and guiding principles for societal participation were further developed in the "Green Book: Participation in research", published in 2021 (based on a large-scale online consultation of experts and previous experiences). From 2021-2022 the BMBF put in place the "Citizens' Assembly on Research" that incorporated the societal perspective into the "Strategy for Participation in Research" . In 2022, the Citizens' Assembly adopted its final report with 25 concrete recommendations and 5 guiding principles. Many of these recommendations were fed into the Strategy. The independent evaluation of the report suggested that citizens' assemblies may be a suitable instrument for the BMBF in the future. Furthermore, a discussion group on participation was set up to focus on the inclusion of the science community. The Alliance of Science Organisations also published a "Statement on Participation" on 9 November 2022. The BMBF "Strategy for Participation in Research" was released in June 2023. Participation in research and research policy has existed for many years, and it is a dynamic field. This is why a mid-term review will be carried out after three years.

Description: The national intellectual property rights strategy (IPR Strategy) has been formulated to develop competences and administration related to intellectual property and to introduce measures to improve the current situation.
Objective(s): In 2030, Finland will have an effective IPR operating environment that supports innovation and creative work, which will increase economic wellbeing and competitiveness by taking into account the realisation of fundamental rights and different social interests in a diverse way.|Finnish actors have strong IPR expertise.|World-class innovations are created and commercialised in Finland|Intellectual property is an integral part of political decision-making|Finland has a functioning and competitive IPR system.|Finland promotes the development of the IPR system and regulation in the EU and internationally.
Background:
Digitalisation is advancing at an accelerating pace and its focus is on the data economy, platform economy and artificial intelligence. The role and importance of data and dataintensive ecosystems, AI and the platform economy are growing rapidly in all business activities. Data are utilised, in particular, by combining data from different sources, and the role of data sharing is growing rapidly.

The politicisation of rights and the increase in conflicts are reflected in the fact that major global trade policy actors increasingly take intellectual property rights into account in their trade policy guidelines. The increase in protectionism caused by the COVID-19 pandemic also has an impact on national strategies for intellectual property, in addition to the ongoing struggle for competitiveness. IPR violations are still on the rise in the digital environment, which is reflected in increased litigation.

The speed of the change and the convergence of fields of law are putting pressure on the flexibility of legislation. Technological progress in particular is very rapid and new business models are emerging at an accelerating pace. The convergence of different fields of law is also increasing. IPR legislation and other fields of law, such as competition law, constitutional law, fundamental and human rights and legislation concerning investment protection, are increasingly intersecting.

Intellectual property rights play a role as a builder and maintainer of global competitiveness. Countries that are able to identify areas of business where they have strong expertise are able to use that expertise to build a stronger global competitive position for their industries and thereby support their economic growth. Such areas may include, for example, the environment, the circular economy and quantum technology.

Description: The Technology Development Center (TEKMER) is a platform that offers services such as business development, access to financial resources, management, consultancy, mentoring, office space, and network participation to entrepreneurs and businesses during pre-incubation, incubation, and post-incubation stages. Additionally, TEKMER supports entrepreneurs and businesses with technology- or innovation-focused ideas or projects involving research and development and/or product, process, or service innovation in one or more related themes.
Objective(s): To establish and operate structures that provide pre-incubation, incubation, and post-incubation services.|To ensure the establishment and sustainability of businesses in R&D, innovation, and technological entrepreneurship.|To foster collaboration among actors in the entrepreneurship ecosystem.
Background:

To support the establishment and sustainability of R&D- and innovation-focused businesses, the TEKMER Support Program was revised in 2020 to create more practical and sustainable TEKMERs based on field demands.
One of the main changes in the last two years is that TEKMERs established under the İŞGEM/TEKMER Support Program are now subject to the TEKMER Support Program for the remaining period. Additionally, expenses approved under the İŞGEM/TEKMER Support Program but not yet paid were increased by 58% without requiring a new board decision.
The program period is 5 years, with a support rate of 75%. The upper limit of support within the scope of the TEKMER Support Program is 6,000,000 TL.
Under the program, support is provided to the operating organization for the following expenses:
• Furniture and equipment,
• Machinery, equipment, and software for shared use,
• Personnel expenses,
• Training, consultancy, organization, and promotion expenses.
In addition, based on TEKMER's needs, additional support of up to 4,000,000 TL can be provided to expand its physical structure for capacity development.
Support Items:
• Furniture and Equipment Support: 2,000,000 TL (non-refundable).
• Shared Use Machinery, Equipment, and Software Support: 2,000,000 TL (non-refundable) and 2,000,000 TL (repayable).

Background:
In the 2021-27 European Union policy programming period, smart specialization strategies and their governance model constitute the only enabling condition for funding Policy Objective 1, which includes support for the development and reinforcement of research and innovation and the adoption of advanced technologies, as well as the development of skills for smart specialization, industrial transition and entrepreneurship.

In order to comply with this enabling condition, the Smart Specialization Strategy for Norte Region 2021-27 (S3 NORTE 2027) was approved on December 30, 2020 by the Regional Council of CCDR-NORTE, appearing in chapter 2 of Norte Region Development Strategy for Programming Period 2021-27 of European Union Policies (NORTE 2030).

Considering that S3 NORTE 2027 is an enabling condition of the Norte Regional Operational Programme (NORTE 2030), the alignment with S3 NORTE 2027 was defined as an admissibility condition and/or a selection criteria (relative and absolute) for some typologies of projects, namely for the Specific Objectives: SO 1.1 “Strengthen research and innovation capacities and the adoption of advanced technologies” and SO 1.3 “Strengthening the sustainable growth and competitiveness of SMEs, as well as job creation” of Policy Objective 1 “A more competitive and smarter Europe”; and SO 4.d “Promoting the adaptation of workers, companies and entrepreneurs to change” of PO 4 “A more social and inclusive Europe”.

The relevant eligible typologies of actions under these SO are:
SO 1.1 - Knowledge and technology transfer (collective actions and public or assimilable technology transfer projects and technological infrastructure projects); Business investment and economic valuation of knowledge (R&TD Incentive Systems and Technological Entrepreneurship);
SO 1.3 - Infrastructure and equipment (non-technologically based) to support competitiveness (business reception areas and social incubators or business incubators).
SO 4.d - Hiring of highly qualified human resources: support for the hiring of highly qualified human resources with fair remuneration and job sustainability perspectives in areas aligned with the priority domains of S3 NORTE 2027: (i) by companies (micro, small and medium); (ii) by scientific and technological infrastructures; (iii) in the context of collective efficiency strategies or the territorialization of S3 NORTE 2027.

English name: Świętokrzyski Laboratory Campus of the Central Office of Measures
Original name(s): Świętokrzyski Kampus Laboratoryjny Głównego Urzędu Miar w Kielcach
Description: The Campus project assumes the construction, in cooperation of the Central Office of Measures with the Kielce University of Technology, of a laboratory research and implementation base, which will allow for effective and professional conduct of research and development work, which will directly affect the intensification of cooperation between the research and scientific sphere and enterprises.
Objective(s): Development and scientific infrastructure created in cooperation with the Kielce University of Technology Campus is to use the science of metrology to increase the competitiveness of Polish companies on the European and global markets and to create a Polish metrology centre.|Contribute to the development of scientific research at national and European level.|Cooperation with academic centres from all over the country, the level of education and awareness of the importance of measurements among academic staff and students.
Background:
The new metrology laboratories will improve research and development processes for determining the uniformity of measures, taking into account the required accuracy of measurements of physical quantities. The project planned for implementation will also enable a qualitative change in the functioning of research units for dynamic interaction with industry and science. The activity of the laboratory campus and its interaction with science and economy will lead to active cooperation of scientific institutions, related to the exchange of technological ideas in the field of innovative methods of measurement and the development of the latest technologies.
The built Campus will contribute to the development of scientific research at national and European level. Equipping laboratories with modern infrastructure, minimizing the impact of environmental conditions and disturbances, increasing technical capabilities in relation to the current state will directly affect the quality of scientific research. This quality will be expressed by performing advanced and non-standard measurements and by ensuring measurement consistency at a world-class level.
The campus will provide a professional didactic base for scientists from Poland and abroad, through which it will provide services of the highest world standard. The activity of the Campus will stop the phenomenon of the so-called "brain drain". This effect will be achieved through the organization of numerous trainings and paid internships abroad, scientific development (doctoral dissertations in cooperation with research centers, publications in scientific journals, participation in domestic and foreign scientific conferences). In addition, direct contacts with international experts cooperating within the EURAMET Technical Committees and CIPM Advisory Councils will ensure our staff participation in European research programs such as EMPIR. Particular support will be given to inventiveness and innovation.
As part of cooperation with academic centers from all over the country, the level of education and awareness of the importance of measurements among academic staff and students will be raised. Cooperation of academic staff with entrepreneurs and enrichment of the labor market with graduates equipped with new competences will make the project conducive to the accumulation of human capital, which will be the basis for stimulating economic development. The equipment and human resources of the Campus will be an attractive contribution to international projects, which will allow for the internationalization of the Campus's scientific and research activities.
The strategic goal of the planned research, development and scientific infrastructure created in cooperation with the Kielce University of Technology Campus is to use the science of metrology to increase the competitiveness of Polish companies on the European and global markets and to create a Polish metrology center, a place where research, scientific and industry-related environments will meet. The basis for achieving such a goal is to adapt the national metrological institution to today's conditions and requirements of the Polish economy.

English name: Smart Growth, Digitalization and Financial Instruments Programme (POCIDIF)
Original name(s): Programul Creștere Inteligentă, Digitalizare și Instrumente Financiare
Description: POCIDIF targets support measures, at the national level, for Research, innovation and digitalization, including in the cultural sector.
Objective(s): Development and strengthening of research and innovation capacities and the adoption of advanced technologies.|Strengthening the sustainable growth and competitiveness of SMEs and creating jobs in SMEs, including through productive investments.|Developing skills for smart specialization, industrial transition and entrepreneurship.
Background:
POCIDIF is structured on 3 Priorities, specific objectives as well as actions and measures to be implemented in order to achieve those objectives.
Priority 1 of POCIDIF (P1) is dedicated to research and innovation in RO - Supporting and promoting an attractive and competitive RDI system in Romania.
P1, RSO1.1. targets 3 types of actions, followed by specific measures, in the smart specialization domains defined within SNCISI, focused on supporting the innovative potential of enterprises and on the creation/development of a competitive ecosystem by making available the expertise of research organizations, including by connecting to the European Research Area.
RSO1.1. Developing and enhancing research and innovation capacities and the uptake of advanced technologies
Action 1.1 Support for the private sector and for collaboration between actors from the public system and the business environment in the field of CDI
Action 1.2 Support for projects in the field of advanced technologies by creating innovation hubs in areas of strategic interest
Action 1.3 Integration of the national RDI ecosystem in the European and international Research Space
Action 1.4. Developing skills and strengthening the capacity of actors in the CDI field in order to ensure increased competitiveness
Action 1.5 Support for increasing the competitiveness of enterprises
Action 1.5.1 Creation/operationalization of a national entrepreneurial HUB
Action 1.5.2 Smart business development: new models for business development and re-engineering Cohesion Policy for 2021 – 2027.

Romania is an emerging innovator. The need to support SMEs, public-private RDI collaboration, increase the capacity to innovate/integrate results in value chains, increase system performance, create knowledge/technology hubs, derives from: low performance in innovation (last place in the EU) ; low RDI investments (0.5% GDP, public 0.2 and private 0.3), below the EU average of 1.4%; lack of vision for the transition to activities with high added value and low SME/inhabitant level; scientific performance and weak university-business linkages; the lack of integrated market research initiatives resulting in areas with a small spillover effect on issues of national interest, especially in the current socio-economic context.

The financed projects in the smart specialization domains identified in SNCISI will ensure the spillover effect being implemented in partnership with entities from all categories of regions, capitalizing on the existing RDI capacity within the research organizations/institutes.
RDI interventions are systemic, the business environment/citizens from all over RO will benefit from innovative products/services with a positive impact on the economy as well as on the quality of life in all types of regions.

In order to accelerate the pace of economic and social transformation, the transfer of the results of research activities to the market is ensured by developing a sustainable, predictable and stable RDI ecosystem, allowing to maximize the leverage effects of public-private cooperation, encouraging interaction between different actors and facilitating the exchange of knowledge and technological transfer between them. POCIDIF proposes to increase/maintain research jobs, create a motivating/attractive environment for young researchers, increase their skills for the transfer of acquired knowledge to the market and, at the same time, technology transfer. SMEs will be supported in order to introduce product/process/service innovation in their own activity as well as the training of their staff and from research organizations in the fields of intelligent specialization, entrepreneurship and industrial transition (industry 4.0), the support of supporting the process of entrepreneurial discovery and of identifying the most relevant projects at national level. The interventions will stimulate research organizations and enterprises for a better positioning on the value chain of innovation, thus creating the premises of an ecosystem in which the correlation in real terms between need and supply is facilitated, with the use of existing infrastructures.
The program will support advanced technologies to facilitate the creation of integrated HUBs, in national smart specialization areas, capable of ensuring the transferability of results and contributing to the growth of the economy, and simultaneously addressing the fragmentation of the C&I system.

The plan was prepared based on the analysis of development needs, the funding priorities from the Partnership Agreement (PA), as well as the relevant strategic documents at the EU level and at the national level (e.g. National Research, Innovation and Smart Specialization Strategy (SNCISI), Analysis of Factors Impeding the Dissemination of Innovation, including Digitalization, Policy Support Facility, eGov Public Policy, Public Services Catalog, Barriers to the Digitalization of the Public and Private Environment in Romania.
