Description: Smart specialization strategy 2029 (S3 2029) is part of the strategic framework defined by the National Development Strategy 2030 and represents the main strategy in the field of research, development and innovation for the period until 2029. The main purpose of the Croatian S3 is to transform the Croatian economy in order to increase its competitiveness by concentrating knowledge resources and linking them to a limited number of priorities.
Objective(s):
Main objective: Enhance Croatia’s research and innovation performance and capacity to boost competitiveness and promote digital and green transformation.|Intermediate objectives:
1. Raising research excellence
2. Bridging the gap between the research and business sector
3. Boosting innovation performance
Background:
S3 2029 builds upon lessons learned during implementation of S3 of the Republic of Croatia for period 2016-2020 and upon S3 2016-2020 mid-term evaluation. Five thematic priority areas (TPA) defined by S3 2016-2020 are broaden into 7 TPAs, where investments from ESI Funds, Recovery and Resilience Facility and national budget will be directed. Seven TPAs are: Personalized Health, Smart and Clean Energy, Smart and Green Transport, Security - Awareness, Prevention, Response, and Remediation, Sustainable and Circular Food, Customized and Integrated Wood .
Products, Digital Products and Platforms.
S3 2029 is conceived as a flexible and "living" strategy that will be adjusted according to future trends and needs of the national innovation system stakeholders. Entrepreneurial discovery process, as a bottom-up process of formal consultation of stakeholders and experts, plays an important role in that respect, as it had in the creation of the Strategy. The strategy foresees turning EDP into a continuous process and to strengthen the governing role of National Innovation Council. NIC will have a better operational (technical and analytical) support in Policy Delivery Unit, which will enable more efficient implementations taken by NIC.

English name: National Guidelines for Knowledge and Technology Transfer
Original name(s): Nacionalne smjernice za transfer znanja i tehnologije
Description: National guidelines for knowledge and technology transfer provide recommendations and practical advice to technology transfer offices (TTOs) and managers in research organizations to improve technology and knowledge transfer activities and results and therefore they represent an important step in the direction of defining and strengthening the position of TTOs in Croatian innovation system.
Objective(s): The objective of the Guidelines is to provide a framework for the effective use of results of publicly funded research through the proper management of intellectual property, increased commercialization, development of entrepreneurial culture and related skills in public scientific organizations and for more successful interaction between the public and business sectors.
Background: In the past 10-15 years, efforts have been made to encourage the transfer of knowledge and technology from research organizations to the business sector – e.g., by establishing of several TT offices in Croatia, by providing grant schemes enabling collaborative science-business projects and schemes directing research organizations to orient towards the needs of enterprises. Nevertheless, a comprehensive analysis showed that the greater momentum was needed in this direction, as well as the systematic development of TT practices at higher education institutions and institutes as well as raising awareness on the potentials and importance of technology and knowledge transfer. Therefore the Guidelines were created.

Description:
Under this Initiative several programs and grant schemes are planned that aim at different aspects of knowledge and technology transfer:
• Technology transfer programs funded from RRF support activities carried out by public research organizations in cooperation with technology transfer offices
• The Technology Transfer Fund (TTF), funded from World Bank loan (DIGIT project), is a strategic initiative designed to support the transfer of technology and knowledge from laboratories and operational environments to the commercial market. The TTF is designed to complement the existing Proof-of-Concept (PoC) program which supports pre-commercial testing of innovative concepts to determine their potential to become commercially viable products or services.
• Technology scouting program, a program providing an ongoing support from scouts or other experts for the development and implementation of Proof of Concept (PoC). Technology scouts offer key services such as business validation and PoC preparation (funded from the DIGIT project)
• Professionalization of research centers program, focusing on professionalizing the management of research infrastructure by establishing clear structures, improving financial management, and strengthening collaboration with the private sector (funded from the DIGIT project)
Objective(s): Increase the number of technology transfer processes at higher education institutions and scientific organizations.
Background: Technology transfer programs implemented by MSEY continue the financing from the previous financial period; Croatian Agency for SMEs, Innovation and Investments (HAMAG-BICRO) handled a call for proposals Support to Technology Transfer Offices (TTO program) with the aim to strengthen the role of technology transfer offices (TTO) at universities and public research institutes in Croatia as central places for stimulating and implementing technology transfer activities. The program was financed through Second Technological Development Project (STP II) a loan from the World Bank in the amount of 1.459.950 EUR.

English name: Act on the Croatian Science Foundation
Original name(s): Zakon o Hrvatskoj zakladi za znanost
Description: The Act more clearly defines the tasks of the Croatian Science Foundation in the field of implementation, coordination, design, monitoring and evaluation of programmes and for evaluating research and development project financing policies, thus creating a strong and independent system for the implementation of the selection, funding and monitoring of research and development projects.
Objective(s): Transformation of the Foundation into a body enabling a simplified and systematic approach to the project financing management policy.|Improving and promoting science and technological development.|Fostering scientific excellence, competitiveness in research funding.|Encouraging national and international cooperation and networking.|Supporting applied research in the public sector and knowledge transfer to the private sector.|Boosting international quality criteria in research, transparency and equality, prevention of conflicts of interest, the highest ethical standards and ensuring academic freedoms.
Background: With the adoption of the Act, the process of restructuring the Foundation began. The restructuring includes the amendment of the basic normative framework of the Foundation, introduction of a new program and monitoring framework, and the strengthening of the Foundation's operational capacities. The Act more clearly regulates the legal status of the Foundation and division of the work of the Foundation's bodies with the aim of increasing the quality and transparency of the financing of scientific projects and programs.

Description:
Investments of the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth (MSEY), listed under special objective 1.i and 1.iv., focus on investing in research, technology, and innovation (RTI) infrastructure to support market-driven research as well as into applied research projects, centres of research excellence, technology transfer, the development of skills for smart specialization, proof of concept and collaborative research between research and business sector.

Priority objective 1. “Strengthening the economy by investing in research and innovation, supporting business competitiveness, digitization and developing skills for smart specialization”.|Specific objectives:

1.iv Developing skills for smart specialization, industrial transition and entrepreneurship.

Description: The State Intellectual Property Office of the Republic of Croatia is the State administration body with responsibilities in the field of protection of intellectual property rights.
Objective(s): Carrying out procedures for granting industrial property rights (patents, trademarks, industrial designs, geographical indications and designations of origin, topographies of semiconductor products) and performs the accompanying professional and legislative activity.|Making the provision of information and services in the field of intellectual property.|Cooperating with other institutions for the enforcement of intellectual property rights and support of innovation activity, as well as the cooperation with economic and R&D entities.
Background:
Since its independence, Croatia has been independently building a national intellectual property protection system in line with contemporary world trends.
The Republic of Croatia ensures high standards of intellectual property protection through its national protection system harmonized with international agreements in the field of intellectual property established under the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and the World Trade Organization (WTO) as well as regional systems and legal framework. National regulations governing the intellectual property protection system are continuously developed and harmonized with the highest international standards and the development of a common legal framework for the protection of intellectual property in the EU.
The basic national regulations are:
• Copyright and Related Rights Act
• Trademark Act
• Patent Act
• Industrial Design Act
• Act on Geographical Indications and Designations of Origin of Products and Services
• Act on the Protection of Topographies of Semiconductor Products
• Act on the Protection of Undisclosed Information with Market Value
In the Republic of Croatia, the coordination mechanism for performance of the tasks and activities related to the enforcement of intellectual property rights was established in 2010. Coordination mechanism is operating on several levels through standing coordinating bodies, coordinating sub-groups and working groups. In this way, a better cooperation between the competent authorities for the enforcement of intellectual property rights in the Republic of Croatia and other institutions, included in the system of IP legal protection, as well as with users of the IP protection system (the right holders), has been provided.

Background: The Joint Programming Initiative Healthy and Productive Seas and Oceans (JPI Oceans) was established in 2011 as an intergovernmental platform, open to all EU Member States and Associated Countries who invest in marine and maritime research. The establishment of JPI Oceans was driven by the growing recognition of the importance of marine and maritime resources for Europe's economy, environment, and security. The increasing complexity and scale of ocean-related challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and marine pollution, required more coordinated and integrated research efforts. Additionally, fragmented national research efforts were seen as inefficient and unable to address global marine issues effectively. The need for a more strategic approach led to the formation of JPI Oceans, which aligns national research priorities and enhances collaboration across Europe.

Original name(s): NPOO pod-komponenta 3.2, Reforma 3: Poboljšanje učinkovitosti javnih ulaganja u području istraživanja, razvoja i inovacija
Description:
Reform envisages setting up and launching a smart, targeted and consistent policy of public investment in research, development and innovation through a new institutional framework for the implementation of competitive support programs that must be fast and connected in terms of innovation processes and adapted to the needs of users (researchers, research institutions and companies). It therefore aims to introduce a more functional RDI project funding programming framework. That is accomplished by designing new and more functional RDI programs such as Proof of Concept, Targeted Scientific Research and Technology Transfer Programs.
Reform implementation included the adoption of a new Act on the Croatian Science Foundation (CSF) in 2022, which enabled the implementation of adapted programs in accordance with the revised research, development and innovation funding framework.
The new legal framework made a basis for transformation and strengthening Foundation into a body that, with clearly agreed and defined competences within the framework of inter-institutional coordination within the National Innovation Council, will enable a simplified and systematic approach to the management policy of RDI project funding. Moreover, new legal framework enabled CSF to be a part of National Innovation Council as well as integral part of Policy Implementation and Monitoring Unit that serves as a focal point for monitoring and evaluation and provides a continuous support to governing body (NIC) by providing analysis related to the performance of the entire research and innovation system, the progress towards the implementation of interventions, the achievement of S3 goals etc and provide administrative and technical support to NIC, TICs and other S3 bodies.
Objective(s): The objective of the reform is to improve the efficiency of public investment in research, development and innovation in Croatia.

Corallia has founded 3 hi-tech Clusters with more than 175 members, consisting of the most innovative enterprises, university labs and research institutes in their respective sectors: the mi-Cluster (nano/microelectronics-based systems and applications cluster) the first innovation cluster in Greece; the si-Cluster (space technologies and applications cluster) aiming to develop Greece as a leading region for space technologies and applications; and the gi-Cluster (gaming and creative technologies & applications cluster) that displays state-of-the-art technology edge coupled with an extrovert, global-reaching entrepreneurial spirit.

As examples in this context, Corallia has supported a series of flagship initiatives to stimulate youth entrepreneurship, including the business accelerator "egg – enter-grow-go" in cooperation with Eurobank, the "Startab: entrepreneurship program in cooperation with the King’s Trust International, and the "ESA BIC Greece" business incubator in collaboration with the European Space Agency.

English name: Research and Innovation Policy Bill 2025-2028 - Research and Innovation for Future, Curiosity and Benefit
Original name(s): Forskning och innovation för framtid, nyfikenhet och nytta
Description: The Government’s Research and Innovation Bill outlines the direction of Sweden’s research policy over the next four years. It contains the major new and strengthened national STI-policy initiatives as well as the budget allocations for these for the coming four years.
Objective(s):
Excellence and competitiveness in groundbreaking technologies
Advanced research infrastructures for excellent research and innovation
Improved mechanisms and incentives for EU and wider international collaborations
Mechanisms for STI-actors to ensure research security (responsible internationalisation)
Development of a new mechanism to allocate basic funding for research at HEI
Background:
The resources will increase considerably over the 4 years covered by the bill. The level of Government R&D-funding will increase by SEK 1.5 billion 2025, SEK 2.5 billion 2026, SEK 4.0 billion 2027 and SEK 6.5 billion 2028. By 2028 that would mean about 15 percent higher level of Government funding of R&D compared to 2024, in current prices.

An important background to the bill is the radid development of emerging, groundbreaking, and strategically important technologies, and that the global competition is becoming increasingly fierce. The EU, the USA, and China have all taken initiatives and are investing significant resources to strengthen their domestic capabilities in technology. Sweden has a highly research- and technology-intensive industry that competes in a global market. Therefore, high-quality research in technology areas is central. The government is now making substantial investments in research and innovation for groundbreaking and strategic technology.

Certain societal challenges also require focused investments in research and innovation, including practice-oriented research. This includes areas such as bioeconomy, environment, and climate, where knowledge and innovation are needed to achieve the green transition in the best possible way. It also includes the health sector, where several challenges both nationally and globally require efforts, and where the life science sector is important for Sweden. It concerns societal areas with significant needs for practice-oriented research and new knowledge, such as crime and social services, as well as in schools and healthcare.

The basis for the investments is excellence, internationalization, and innovation. Sweden should be an internationally attractive country for investments in research and development. The government believes that Sweden should be among the leading countries in terms of research and development (R&D) expenditure as a percentage of GDP. To achieve this, not only is a substantial investment in resources needed, but also an increase in ambition with a clearer focus on excellence.

Policy instrument type: Competitive Grants to Universities and Colleges for Research and Education at the Doctoral Level
Policy instrument name:
COMPETITIVE GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES FOR RESEARCH AND EDUCATION AT THE DOCTORAL LEVEL
It is important that increased research grants, like other investments in research, are distributed in such a way that they contribute to achieving the overarching goals of excellence, innovation, and internationalization. The government therefore intends to allocate increased funds to research grants to the areas and institutions that can best meet the goals. The model for quality-based distribution of research grants introduced in 2009 continues to be the basis for distribution, but is adjusted in some parts to further increase competition for funds between institutions to increasingly reward quality.
The majority of state-funded research is conducted at universities and colleges. Like in other leading research countries, research in Sweden is funded through a mix of direct grants for research and education at the doctoral level to the institutions and external contributions from public and private financiers. The proportion of direct grants varies between countries. In Sweden, it is on average less than half of the total research funding for institutions. Direct grants strengthen the institutions' long-term conditions and provide incentives in strategically important areas such as employment and research infrastructure. The grants provide a foundation for building research environments and research groups that can attract international expertise and better compete for external research funds. External research funds also sometimes require co-financing from the institutions, for example, when it comes to funds from the EU and certain private financiers. This is financed with the direct grants. Direct grants are also crucial for research in areas where access to external funds is low.

Motives
In a new geopolitical reality, emerging and groundbreaking technologies have the potential to become a significant factor and a means of power. Therefore, high-quality research in technology areas is central. Old divisions of different research areas are becoming less significant, the boundaries between basic research and applied research are becoming increasingly difficult to draw, and the boundary between civil and military research is being reconsidered more often as research and its results can have dual uses, so-called dual use. Groundbreaking technologies have the potential to provide significant positive effects on competitiveness, societal development, and prosperity. Sweden therefore needs to mobilize and enable research, innovation, and development in such areas.
The government is therefore making an investment amounting to just over 1.2 billion SEK annually from 2028 in excellence clusters for groundbreaking technology. This broad investment aims to cover both early-stage technology research and innovation and application in later stages of technology development and therefore goes through both the Swedish Research Council and Vinnova.
Excellence Clusters
The investment in excellence clusters should lead to the development of future technology areas and strategic technology areas that can strengthen Swedish industry and, in the long term, Sweden's competitiveness. Furthermore, the investment is expected to increase the long-term supply of skills in various technology areas that are of great importance for Swedish competitiveness and societal development.
Excellence clusters mean that resources are concentrated and researchers from different universities are mobilized to provide good conditions for successful national and international collaborations in important emerging and strategic technology areas. The program includes both an open part funded by the Swedish Research Council and a strategic part funded by Vinnova. These two parts should be coordinated through a joint program office.
The investment in excellence clusters should lead to state funds creating a leverage effect together with industry R&D investments and contribute to research results being transformed into commercial products and services. This also includes small and medium-sized enterprises that have a long growth journey to commercialization and large capital needs in early stages.
Swedish Research Council
The Swedish Research Council's part of the investment in Excellence Clusters for groundbreaking technology will focus on future technology areas.. Each cluster will encompass a powerful and focused investment of 20–40 million SEK per cluster per year. The investment enables Swedish universities with the highest scientific quality in each technology area to collaborate and push the frontier forward for these technology areas with the goal of becoming internationally leading.
Within the framework of the Swedish Research Council's budget increase, 125 million SEK will be allocated in 2025 for the investment in excellence clusters for groundbreaking technology with a focus on future technologies. Subsequently, 265 million SEK in 2026, 420 million SEK in 2027, and 710 million SEK in 2028 are estimated for this purpose. Of this investment, at least 100 million SEK will be directed towards AI by 2028. The investment will also include research schools for AI, groundbreaking technology, and STEM.
Vinnova
Vinnova's part of the investment in Excellence Clusters for strategic technology will focus on strategic technology areas where Sweden already has a strong position that needs to be secured, new groundbreaking technology areas where Sweden needs to build competence and take a position, or technology areas of importance to reduce vulnerability and increase resilience against various threats. The investment builds on experiences and collaboration forms in the strategic innovation programs created through previous research policy propositions.
Within the framework of Vinnova's budget increase, 62 million SEK will be allocated in 2025 for the investment in groundbreaking technology, focusing on strategically important technology areas. Subsequently, 143 million SEK in 2026, 268 million SEK in 2027, and 537 million SEK in 2028 are estimated for this purpose.
Program Office
The government intends to assign the Swedish Research Council and Vinnova to establish a joint program office to coordinate calls that include both the Swedish Research Council's and Vinnova's calls within excellence clusters for emerging and groundbreaking technology. The program office should also ensure that investments are made across all technology maturity stages, from basic research to innovation. Evaluation of the investments should also be part of the program office's tasks. The Swedish Research Council and Vinnova should work towards synergies between the investments where relevant. They should also utilize opportunities for international collaborations and programs, especially within the EU.

Policy instrument name:
STRENTHENING OF MAX IV
MAX IV is an X-ray facility for materials and life science research and a world-leading synchrotron facility. Lund University hosts the facility, which is a national research infrastructure that was commissioned in 2016. MAX IV currently has sixteen instruments, known as beamlines, each specialized in studying different properties of materials. In addition to the existing beamlines, there is space for twelve more beamlines. The facility is used for research on new materials and pharmaceuticals, as well as advanced analytical methods in areas such as nanotechnology and quantum materials. In total, the facility has approximately 1,700 users from 34 countries and 280 different organizations within both academia and industry. The number of users has steadily increased since 2022, particularly from industry, which, due to the green transition, has a need for advanced materials research.

The government sees the need to create conditions for long-term and stable operation, maintaining a high-quality user program, and enabling strategic development of MAX IV. Strategic upgrades and more instruments are of great importance if the facility is to remain world-leading. As new instruments are installed, the operating costs for the facility will increase.

Within the framework of the Swedish Research Council's budget increase for research, 50 million SEK will be allocated in 2025 to strengthen MAX IV. Subsequently, 55 million SEK in 2026, 65 million SEK in 2027, and 90 million SEK in 2028 are estimated for this purpose.

SCIENTIFIC AND SOCIAL BENEFITS OF ESS AND MAX IV
Sweden has made significant investments in the research facilities ESS and MAX IV over several years. To ensure that Sweden gains the maximum benefit from these investments in the form of excellent research, technological development, innovations, and utilization, there is a need to ensure the systematic build-up of knowledge and competence for the development and use of the facilities within universities, colleges, industry, and other sectors. The government is therefore allocating additional resources to the Swedish Research Council to implement strategic initiatives that promote the scientific and societal benefits of ESS, MAX IV, and international large-scale research infrastructure in which Sweden is a member. The initiative may include, for example, a graduate school with industrial doctoral students, Swedish involvement in upcoming instruments at ESS, accessibility for new user groups, and the promotion of Swedish participation in technology development projects at international research facilities. The initiative includes ensuring that the Swedish Research Council systematically follows up on the socio-economic effects of ESS and MAX IV.

Within the framework of the Swedish Research Council's budget increase for research, 35 million SEK will be allocated in 2025 for measures that promote and enable the follow-up of the scientific and societal benefits of ESS and MAX IV. Subsequently, 35 million SEK in 2026, 45 million SEK in 2027, and 55 million SEK in 2028 are estimated for this purpose.

STRENGTHENING SciLifeLab
Science for Life Laboratory, SciLifeLab, is a national center for molecular biosciences jointly operated by the Royal Institute of Technology, Karolinska Institute, Stockholm University, and Uppsala University. The center operates at several universities across the country and offers various technologies along with expertise that enables groundbreaking research in a range of research areas. SciLifeLab has established national programs for laboratory pandemic preparedness, precision medicine, environmental research, and the development of future drug candidates.

This is an important part of making Sweden a leading life science nation, as expressed in the updated national life science strategy (KN2024/02228) and is a clear goal in the government's work. Strong knowledge and research environments have been established throughout the country through SciLifeLab, attracting technical experts, research talents, and international collaborations. This broad foundation in excellent research environments makes SciLifeLab unique, even from an international perspective. Through SciLifeLab, Sweden has taken a leading position in several European collaborative projects in data-driven life sciences and AI, such as the European test and demonstration facility for AI in health and the European genomics data infrastructure.

To succeed in tough global competition, it is crucial that researchers in Sweden have access to the most advanced technologies and expertise in the future. The government therefore considers it of utmost importance to support and further develop SciLifeLab as a national resource and ensure a wide range of cutting-edge technologies, expertise, and conditions for excellent research in life sciences.

In the budget proposal for 2025, the government proposes and estimates an increase in the funding for universities and colleges for research and education at the doctoral level. Within these funds, 90 million SEK will be allocated in 2025 to the Royal Institute of Technology's funding for research and education at the doctoral level to strengthen SciLifeLab. Subsequently, 90 million SEK in 2026, 90 million SEK in 2027, and 90 million SEK in 2028 are estimated for this purpose.

DIGITAL RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE
Just like in other parts of society, the digitization of research is a strong driving force for rapid development, while the demands for technical infrastructure for processing, analysis, storage, and accessibility of research data are increasing. More and more of the research source material, methods, and tools are becoming digital, which creates societal benefits.

Overall, this means that the needs for digital research infrastructure, i.e., storage, analysis, and large-scale computing resources, are increasing within both research, the public sector, and industry. The digital research infrastructure, also known as e-infrastructure, needs to be built up and financed in all areas to enable Swedish research and meet the increased need for computing resources, data storage, handling of sensitive data, and increased demands for open research data.

The Swedish Research Council has several tasks related to digital research infrastructure and research data. Among other things, the authority is responsible for the communication system Swedish University Computer Network (Sunet) and coordinates the work for open access to research data in Sweden. Furthermore, the council will coordinate and promote national engagement in the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC). It is important at the national level to contribute to increased utilization of research data that follows the so-called FAIR principles, i.e., that research data should be searchable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and to create conditions for sharing research results and data that can be made available to other researchers and actors within society and industry. In August 2024, the government also tasked the Swedish Research Council with proposing how Swedish e-infrastructure for research can be developed through coordination and organizational change (U2024/01858). The assignment is to be finalized by June 15, 2025.

English name: Lighthouse Projects – Reducing Time to Market
Original name(s): Leitprojekte – Schnelle Umsetzung für den Markt
Description: Fraunhofer is tackling the current challenges facing industry head on. Its lighthouse projects put the focus on strategic objectives with a view to developing practical solutions from which economies such as Germany’s can benefit.
Objective(s): By pooling expertise and involving industrial partners at an early stage, the Fraunhofer Institutes involved in the projects aim to turn original scientific ideas into marketable products as quickly as possible.
Background:
The topics these projects address are geared towards economic requirements. They include the following flagship projects:

- Electrocaloric heat pumps
Description: Development of a new type of heat pump with electrocaloric medium to replace heatpumps with a compressor using toxic F-gases.

- Empathetic technical systems for resilient production
Description: The project aims to demonstrate, for the first time, how the newly intro-duced concept of "empathic production systems" enables more effective and efficient cooperation between actors in production as well as the transformation towards resilient value communities.

- Comprehensive approaches for the evaluation and development of integral car body concepts for sustainable vehicle manufacturing
Description: Development of comprehensive approaches to assess new and integral car body concepts for sustainable manufacturing in the automotive industry.

- Coupled agricultural systems for a resilient and sustainable production of high-quality food proteins
Description: Development of new cultivation systems, which can produce nutritious pro-teins from selected plants, insects, fungi and algae.

- Materials for sustainable tandem solar cells with extremely high conversion efficiency
Description: Development of sustainable, highly efficient and cost-effective tandem solar cells based on new absorber materials.

- NeuroOSmart
Description: The Fraunhofer Flagship Project NeurOSmart aims to set a new standard for intelligent hybrid computing architectures for autonomous technologies by combining a high-performance sensor system, AI-supported pre-processing and a novel high-performance, analog-neuromorphic, ultra-low-power in-memory accelerator chip within one system.

- Automated production of mRNA therapeutics
Description: Develop an AI-driven, automated production process for mRNA therapeutic.

- Shaping the future of green chemistry by process intensification and digitalization
Description: Green, sustainable chemistry contributes to this trend reversal by significant-ly reducing the consumption of non-renewable resources and energy, and by minimizing the use and production of harmful substances, without compromising the economic efficiency of chemical processes or the quality of their products.

- Sustainable biobased and biohybrid materials
Description: Biotransformation of plastics technology by biobased material building blocks utilizing their exclusive molecular functionalities.

- Hierarchical swarms as production architecture with optimized utilization
Description: Create the basis for a manufacturing environment that includes modular manufacturing units which collaborate with similar or different tools, machines or vehi-cles in swarms.

- 6G SENTINEL - the next generation of mobile communication
Description: In the Fraunhofer Flagship Project 6G SENTINEL, five Fraunhofer Institutes are developing key technologies for the impending 6G mobile communications standard, further improving the data rates, availability, accuracy, service quality and reliability and standardization.

- Experimental vertical take-off and landing glider
Description: Airborne experimental platform will be developed and approved for testing and demonstration flights that combines the VTOL capabilities of multicopters with the aerodynamic advantages of gliders.

- A comprehensive process for building refurbishment that is sustainable, modular, and circular
Description: Development of a comprehensive process for building refurbishment that is sustainable, modular and primarily focused on increasing productivity while reducing costs and improving the circularity and carbon neutrality of materials and systems."

- Green ammonia as a decentralized, cross-sector energy vector for the German energy transition
Description: The focus is on ammonia as an energy vector, which in its liquid form can be transported easily and without great energy expenditure thereby addressing the en-tire value chain: reactors and catalysts for flexible, energy-efficient ammonia synthesis as well as technologies for splitting ammonia and using it to generate electricity, heat and motion. Storage and logistics concepts are also being created and business models de-veloped.

- Digital ecosystem for a resilient and sustainable supply of functionally reliable materials
Description: The initiative combines state-of-the art technologies from experimental approaches to digital solutions to create a digital ecosystem that enhances the resilience and sustainability of the supply of functional-safe materials.

Description: National Action Plan for the European Research Area (ERA) lays the foundation for the strategic direction of German EU research and innovation policy and its implementation until 2027.
Objective(s):
The ERA Action Plan outlines how the Federal Government further advances and fulfils the objectives of the European Research Area by taking national action. In this context, it is important to join forces and pool national efforts with European partners in order to ensure that Europe:

- maintains and boosts its competitiveness, including through the translation of research results into applications; contributes to overcoming the major challenges of our time with basic and applied research and innovation; and generates European added value;
- remains one of the most attractive locations for science in the world, and preserves and enhances its ability to attract talent from around the world;
- further facilitates mobility within the European Research Area;
- shapes and participates in global knowledge flows and innovation processes, through close European and international ties; and
- protects academic freedom and research security in European and international cooperation.

Description: The German Marine Research Alliance (DAM) is a collaborative initiative that strengthens the sustainable use of coasts, seas and oceans through research, transfer, data management and digitalisation. It coordinates infrastructures to optimise their utilisation and operation, excluding research vessels. DAM serves as a platform to develop practical knowledge and orientation for politics, business and civil society to support sustainability and ocean protection.

Background: Founded in 2019 by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and northern German states, DAM unites leading German marine research institutions. DAM aims to provide a foundation for the necessary transition towards greater sustainability and ocean protection by delivering orientation and practical knowledge to politics, business and civil society.
